content: The systolic blood pressure represents the pressure within the blood vessels when the heart contracts or beats. The diastolic blood pressure, on the other hand, reflects the pressure in the blood vessels when the heart is at rest between beats. Hypertension, commonly referred to as high blood pressure, is a significant medical condition that markedly increases the risk of developing diseases affecting the heart, brain, kidneys, and other vital organs. Hypertension is defined based on specific systolic and diastolic blood pressure thresholds or the documented use of antihypertensive medications. Globally, approximately 4 billion people are affected by hypertension, yet only 14% of these individuals have their condition adequately controlled. Despite this, cost-effective treatment options are available. The World Health Organization (WHO) last published a guideline specifically addressing elevated blood pressure in 1999, which is now outdated. In 2007, a comprehensive guideline on cardiovascular risk included some recommendations on hypertension, but this too requires revision and updating in light of new evidence and clinical practices. There is a particular need for guidance on controversial issues, such as the appropriate timing for initiating treatment and whether laboratory testing or cardiovascular risk assessment is necessary before starting therapy. Over the past decade, WHO has incorporated the diagnosis and management of hypertension into a broader cardiovascular risk approach as part of the WHO Package of Essential Noncommunicable Disease Interventions (WHO PEN) in 2007, 2010, and 2013. However, this approach has not integrated the most recent advancements in pharmacological treatments. The WHO Essential Medicines List (EML) identifies all major classes of antihypertensive drugs—angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors (ACE inhibitors), calcium channel blockers (CCBs), angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs), and thiazide diuretics—as essential medications. In June 2019, the EML also included single-pill combination medications for hypertension, further supporting the evaluation of all antihypertensive drug classes and single-pill combinations in the current guideline. The 2021 WHO hypertension guideline aims to provide the most up-to-date, evidence-based global public health recommendations on initiating pharmacological treatment for hypertension in adults. These recommendations are targeted at the general adult, non-pregnant, hypertensive population. While many countries and professional societies have developed hypertension guidelines, these are often specific to the population or healthcare setting of that particular country or organization. Recent shifts in hypertension management, such as moving away from beta-blockers as first-line agents and the growing adoption of combination therapies and single-pill combinations, underscore the need for updated global guidance. This guideline for the pharmacological treatment of hypertension in adults is the first global guideline on this topic in over two decades and is particularly relevant to lowand middle-income countries (LMICs). It introduces new recommendations on the thresholds for initiating pharmacological treatment, follow-up intervals, target blood pressure levels for control, and the cadre of healthcare workers authorized to initiate treatment. It also provides a framework for deciding whether to start treatment with monotherapy, dual therapy, or single-pill combinations, and offers guidance for countries on selecting medications for hypertension control in their national guidelines. The guideline does not address the measurement or diagnosis of hypertension but focuses on pharmacotherapy for individuals with a confirmed diagnosis of hypertension, such as those with elevated blood pressure documented on two separate occasions. Although it does not address modifiable risk factors for hypertension, such as unhealthy diets, physical inactivity, tobacco and alcohol use, and obesity, a comprehensive treatment plan for hypertension must include addressing these risk factors through lifestyle modifications and other interventions. Non-pharmacological approaches to managing or preventing hypertension include reducing salt intake to less than 5 grams daily, increasing fruit and vegetable consumption, engaging in regular physical activity, avoiding tobacco use, reducing alcohol consumption, limiting foods high in saturated fats, and eliminating or reducing trans fats in the diet. The guideline does not cover hypertensive crises, as its focus is on chronic blood pressure management in routine care settings. Its objectives include providing blood pressure thresholds for initiating treatment, determining the need for laboratory tests or cardiovascular risk assessments before starting treatment, identifying the pharmacological agents to initiate therapy, deciding on monotherapy versus combination therapy, setting blood pressure control targets, establishing follow-up intervals, and defining the role of non-physician healthcare workers in hypertension management. The primary audience for this guideline includes clinicians and healthcare providers at all levels of care. Secondary audiences include national noncommunicable disease (NCD) and cardiovascular disease (CVD) program managers, healthcare academics, policymakers, students, and manufacturers of hypertension medications. To develop this guideline, WHO established three groups: an internal WHO Steering Group to coordinate the process, a Guideline Development Group (GDG) composed of experts in hypertension and related fields, and an External Review Group (ERG) to provide peer review and ensure alignment with global needs. The GDG developed an analytical framework to assess the impact of interventions on intermediate and final outcomes and formulated Population, Intervention, Comparison, and Outcome (PICO) questions to guide systematic reviews. These reviews informed the guideline development process, with evidence rated for certainty using the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) approach. The GDG rated the certainty of evidence as high, moderate, low, or very low, based on factors such as risk of bias, inconsistency, imprecision, indirectness, and publication bias. Recommendations were categorized as strong or conditional, depending on the balance of desirable and undesirable effects. The GDG reached unanimous consensus on all recommendations, which were informed by evidence-to-decision tables addressing factors such as resource use, equity, acceptability, and feasibility. The development of this guideline was financially supported by the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and WHO. It replaces previous guidance in the WHO PEN package and the HEARTS technical package, focusing on pharmacological treatment thresholds and preferred therapies for hypertension. While it does not address non-pharmacological interventions or hypertensive crises, it provides a robust framework for managing chronic hypertension in routine care settings.
